core: Price control as a government-set legal limit on price: a price ceiling (legal maximum) and a price floor (legal minimum)
Binding vs non-binding: a ceiling only bites when set below equilibrium; a floor only bites when set above equilibrium; otherwise the control has no effect
A binding price ceiling holds price below equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a persistent shortage results
A binding price floor holds price above equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a persistent surplus results
Why a control prevents the market from clearing: the price is not free to adjust, so the surplus or shortage does not melt away
Side effects of a binding ceiling beyond the raw shortage: queues, quality decline, reduced maintenance, and black/secondary markets (rent control example)
Light introduction of deadweight loss: a binding control blocks mutually beneficial transactions and reduces total surplus
supporting: Rent control as the standard price-ceiling illustration; minimum wage and agricultural price supports as standard price-floor illustrations
The positive result (binding ceiling -> shortage; binding floor -> surplus) is settled; the desirability of rent control or a minimum-wage increase is a contested normative/policy question
A concrete dated price-floor figure: the U.S. federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour, in effect since July 24, 2009
outOfScope: The mechanics of equilibrium itself and the market-clearing adjustment process (owned by market-equilibrium; referenced only)
Derivation of the demand and supply curves and the shift-vs-movement distinction (owned by the demand and supply topics)
Elasticity and how the size of a shortage/surplus depends on responsiveness (owned by the elasticity topic)
Deep labor-market analysis of the minimum wage, monopsony, and employment elasticities (owned by the labor-markets topic; named and handed off)
Full consumer-surplus/producer-surplus welfare geometry (introduced only lightly here)

claims.claim: A price control is a law by which a government regulates a price instead of letting supply and demand determine it; the two forms are a price ceiling (a legal maximum price) and a price floor (a legal minimum price).

A price ceiling has an effect only when it is set below the equilibrium price (binding); a ceiling set at or above equilibrium is non-binding and changes nothing. Symmetrically, a price floor bites only when set above equilibrium.

When a binding price ceiling keeps the market price from rising to equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage results; because the price cannot rise, the shortage persists rather than clearing.
When a binding price floor keeps the market price from falling to equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus results; because the price cannot fall, the surplus persists.

In OpenStax's rental-housing illustration, equilibrium is $500 for 15,000 units; a $500 ceiling imposed after demand rises (which would have pushed equilibrium to $600 and 17,000 units) leaves quantity supplied at 15,000 while quantity demanded reaches 19,000, a shortage of 4,000 units.

A binding price ceiling produces side effects beyond the raw shortage: with more buyers than units, non-price rationing appears (queues, waiting lists, favoritism), landlords cut maintenance and convert units, and quality declines even though the posted price is lower.

Both a binding price ceiling and a binding price floor block transactions that willing buyers and sellers would otherwise have made, reducing total (social) surplus; that lost surplus is deadweight loss.
The U.S. federal minimum wage is a price floor for labor set at $7.25 per hour, in effect since July 24, 2009 under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

The welfare and employment effects of raising the minimum wage are genuinely contested and uncertain: CBO's July 2019 analysis estimated a $15-by-2025 federal minimum would raise pay for at least 17 million workers and lift about 1.3 million people out of poverty, while costing a median of about 1.3 million jobs, with a range from near zero to 3.7 million; empirical studies span from little employment effect to substantial job loss.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether binding price controls such as rent control and minimum-wage increases are, on balance, good policy.
positions: The positive prediction that a binding ceiling creates a shortage and a binding floor creates a surplus is not in dispute among economists.

Whether the distributional benefits (lower posted rents, higher pay for those who keep jobs, poverty reduction) outweigh the costs (shortages, quality decline, lost jobs, deadweight loss) is a normative/policy judgment on which economists disagree, partly because the empirical magnitudes are uncertain.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the positive result plainly and flags the desirability of specific controls as a contested normative debate, citing CBO's own range of estimates rather than declaring a policy winner.
